planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, dry, well-drained soil in full sun; silky aster is adapted to poor, gravelly, or sandy prairie soil and performs best without extra fertility or moisture, which encourage floppy growth.

directions: Plant in lean, dry, well-drained soil in full sun; highly drought-tolerant once established and prone to flopping or declining in overly rich or moist soil. Silky aster is a compact native prairie perennial named for the fine, silvery, silky hairs that densely cover its narrow gray-green leaves, giving the whole plant a soft, shimmering appearance that stands out from other fall-blooming asters. In late summer and fall, the wiry stems are covered in a profusion of small, vivid violet-purple, gold-centered flowers that make an excellent late-season nectar source for native bees and migrating monarch butterflies. Its diminutive size and drought tolerance make it a good choice for the front of a dry, sunny prairie planting, rock garden, or gravel bed where richer soil would cause taller, floppier asters to sprawl. Zone 3–8.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; smooth aster tolerates a wide range of soils, from lean prairie ground to average garden soil, and is one of the more adaptable native asters for general garden use.

directions: Plant in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and generally sturdy and self-supporting without staking. Symphyotrichum laeve (smooth aster, or smooth blue aster) is a native tallgrass prairie perennial distinguished by its smooth, waxy, blue-green foliage — a notable contrast to the coarser, hairier leaves of many other native asters — and its clouds of lavender-blue, yellow-centered flowers that open from late summer into fall. It is considered one of the most valuable late-season native asters for pollinators, providing critical nectar for native bees, honeybees, and migrating monarch butterflies as they refuel for their journey south, and it also serves as a larval host plant for pearl crescent butterflies. Its sturdy, upright habit and long fall bloom period make it an excellent choice for the middle of a sunny native perennial border or prairie-style planting, zone 3–8.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, dry, sandy or rocky, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; stiff aster is adapted to poor, thin soils over rock or sand and struggles in rich, moist garden beds.

directions: Plant in lean, dry, sandy or gravelly, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; thrives in poor, thin soil that would stress most perennials and declines in fertile, moist garden conditions. Ionactis linariifolius (stiff aster, also called sandpaper aster for its rough-textured leaves) is a compact, wiry native perennial of dry rocky outcrops, sandy barrens, and open pine woods across eastern North America, forming a low, bushy mound of narrow, needle-like, evergreen leaves quite different in texture from the broader leaves of most asters. In late summer and fall, the stiff stems are topped with numerous small, violet-purple, yellow-centered flowers that provide valuable late nectar for native bees and butterflies. Its tolerance of poor, dry, rocky soil and compact size make it an excellent, low-maintenance choice for a rock garden, dry sunny bank, or gravel planting where richer-soil perennials would fail, zone 3–8.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; bushy aster tolerates both moist and moderately dry conditions and adapts well to a range of garden soils, from meadow edges to lightly shaded borders.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; pinch or shear by a third in early summer to encourage a bushier, more floriferous, self-supporting habit. Symphyotrichum dumosum (bushy aster, or rice button aster) is a native perennial of meadows, open woodland edges, and roadsides across the eastern United States, forming a dense, twiggy, well-branched mound covered from late summer into fall with an abundance of small, numerous, pale lavender to white, yellow-centered flowers — the profusion of small blooms, densely packed like rice grains along the stems, gives rise to the 'rice button' common name. Its adaptability to both sun and partial shade, and to a range of soil moisture levels, makes it one of the more versatile native asters for different garden situations, and the late, long-lasting bloom period provides valuable nectar for native bees and migrating butterflies when few other plants are still flowering. A reliable, easy native for the middle or front of a sunny to lightly shaded fall border, zone 4–8.

planting.note: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed into lean, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; silverleaf sunflower is native to Texas Gulf Coast sand dunes and prairies and thrives in poor, sandy, drought-prone soil, self-seeding readily where conditions suit it.

directions: Sow directly in lean, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; highly drought-tolerant once established and best grown without extra fertility, which promotes weak, floppy growth. Helianthus argophyllus (silverleaf sunflower) is a striking native annual sunflower endemic to the Texas Gulf Coast, instantly recognizable for its densely silver-white, velvety, felted foliage and stems — a dramatic textural and color contrast to the green foliage of nearly every other garden sunflower. Large, bright yellow, brown-centered flower heads open over a long summer season atop the tall, branching, silvery stalks, drawing bees, butterflies, and, later, seed-eating songbirds like goldfinches to the ripening seed heads. As a true coastal-plain native, it tolerates poor sandy soil, salt spray, and drought exceptionally well, making it a strong choice for a Gulf Coast xeriscape, dune-style planting, or wildlife garden. It self-seeds readily in favorable conditions, often persisting as a reseeding annual once established, zone 7–11.
